speakers.name: Dr John Morrison
speakers.title: Associate Professor of Criminology, Maynooth University; Co-Editor in Chief, Behavioral Sciences of Terrorism and Political Aggression
speakers.bio: Dr John Morrison is an Associate Professor of Criminology at Maynooth University, Ireland. He is co-Editor in Chief of the journal Behavioral Sciences of Terrorism and Political Aggression. With a multi-disciplinary background, John's research interests include organisational fragmentation, individual disengagement, and the role of trust in the psychology of terrorism.

title: The Filtering Role of Trust in the Process of Disengagement
description: In this webinar, Dr John Morrison will focus on the role which trust plays within the process of disengagement from violent extremism. Dr Morrison will utilise the Phoenix model of disengagement and deradicalisation as a basis for his presentation. This model includes the theme of (dis)trust as a filter variable. Dr Morrison will critically discuss the implication of this and how it can be integrated within appropriate CVE approaches, including consideration of the need to understand cross-cultural differences in the development and maintenance of trust, and how this may impact our approaches and understanding of disengagement processes.

title: Legacies of 9/11: 25 Years of Changing Global Security
description: A week-long series of panel discussions that marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks, presented by the AVERT Research Network with partner organisations including ANU, Moonshot, Macquarie University, and the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.

speakers.name: Galen Lamphere-Englund
speakers.title: Senior Counter-Terrorism & Conflict Prevention Advisor; Co-Founder & Convener, Extremism and Gaming Research Network (EGRN)
speakers.bio: Galen Lamphere-Englund is a senior advisor with over 16 years’ experience at the intersection of counter-terrorism, violence prevention, and technology. After leading initiatives in more than 30 countries, Galen has advised the United Nations, FBI, INTERPOL, CEPOL, governments, and major technology platforms on preventing online and offline harms, countering violent extremism, and strengthening digital safety. As co-founder of the Extremism and Gaming Research Network, Galen focuses on building safer digital ecosystems across gaming platforms and protecting those who work to keep them secure. Galen recently led the Christchurch Call Foundation’s Project Catalyst, a large-scale consortium dedicated to rapid pilots combating online violent misogyny and TFGBV linked to terrorism and extremism. His work focuses on protecting online ecosystems and advancing practical strategies to prevent terrorist and extremist exploitation of emerging technologies.

speakers.name: Emily Thompson
speakers.title: Principal Strategic Advisor, Christchurch Call Foundation; Extremism and Gaming Research Network
speakers.bio: Emily Thompson is an expert on the exploitation of digital platforms, social media, and gaming spaces by violent extremists and terrorists. As an experienced researcher, consultant and program director, she works to build understanding and resilience against hateful and harmful ideologies that threaten civil society. Emily combines subject matter expertise in terrorist and violent extremist content with curriculum and program development to design effective, innovative, educational programming. She is a Principal Strategic Advisor for the Christchurch Call Foundation, leading the development of a resource hub for caring adults to build understanding of online harms in digital gaming spaces, with actionable strategies to support young people to navigate these areas in safer ways. Emily is a member of the Extremism and Gaming Research Network.

speakers.name: Dr Linda Schlegel
speakers.title: PostDoc, Peace Research Institute Frankfurt (PRIF)
speakers.bio: Dr. Linda Schlegel is a PostDoc at the Peace Research Institute Frankfurt (PRIF), where she co-leads project RadiGaMe - Radicalization on Gaming Platforms and Messenger Services. As a founding member of the Extremism and Gaming Research Network (EGRN), she has researched the intersection of gaming and (counter-)extremism for years, including extremist exploitation of gaming platforms, gamification, and gaming-related prevention and intervention efforts.

speakers.name: Odhran McCarthy
speakers.title: New York Liaison Officer, United Nations Interregional Crime and Justice Research Institute (UNICRI)
speakers.bio: Mr. Odhran McCarthy is the New York Liaison Officer for the United Nations Interregional Crime and Justice Research Institute (UNICRI), based at United Nations Headquarters in New York City. In this role, he supports institutional engagement, partnerships, and programme development, while contributing to UNICRI’s research and operational work across a range of crime, justice, and security issues, with a particular focus on cybercrime and online harms.

title: Behind the Screen: How Terrorists Exploit Gaming Platforms and Online Spaces
description:
Gaming has become central to how people connect, socialize, and build community online, with over 3 billion players globally. Increasingly, however, these same spaces are being exploited by terrorists and individuals or groups promoting violent extremism conducive to terrorism, who use gaming platforms for recruitment, radicalization, propaganda, and financing. Furthermore, the convergence of digital environments, algorithmic amplification, and the social and developmental vulnerabilities of children and youth has created conditions in which harmful content can reach users at scale.

According to research by the United Nations Interregional Crime and Justice Research Institute (UNICRI) and the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism (UNOCT), terrorists are increasingly exploiting gaming-adjacent spaces - such as in-game chats, livestreams, and user-generated content - to spread propaganda and amplify their influence. Furthermore, a Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate (CTED) Trends Alert highlights that, given the powerful and seamless social connectivity of these digital ecosystems, youth and children are also targeted across terrorist ideologies. In Europe and North America, children account for 42 per cent of terror related investigations.

This webinar aims to go behind the screen and provide a clearer picture of these environments. Speakers from CTED’s Global Research Network (GRN) and United Nations entities will explain how features and cultures unique to gaming platforms – combined with AI and other emerging technologies – allow terrorists and groups promoting violent extremism conducive to terrorism to operate undetected.

This webinar is hosted by the Addressing Violent Extremism and Radicalization to Terrorism (AVERT) Research Network, a member of CTED's Global Research Network (GRN), in cooperation with CTED.

speakers.name: Lydia Khalil
speakers.title: Senior Research Fellow, Alfred Deakin Institute; Project Director, Lowy Institute
speakers.bio: Lydia Khalil is a Senior Research Fellow at the Alfred Deakin Institute and a Project Director at the Lowy Institute. In her capacity at Deakin University, she also served as Co-Convenor of the AVERT Research Network and as liaison to the Research and Evaluation Working Group (REWG) of CVESC. As part of her work with the Lowy Institute, Lydia manages the Transnational Challenges Program and Digital Threats to Democracy Project.

speakers.name: Dr Keiran Hardy
speakers.title: Associate Professor, School of Criminology and Criminal Justice, Griffith University
speakers.bio: Dr Keiran Hardy is an Associate Professor in the School of Criminology and Criminal Justice at Griffith University and a member of the Griffith Criminology Institute. He is a recognised expert in counter-terrorism and national security law. He is the author of Law in Australian Society: An Introduction to Principles and Process (Routledge, 2024, 2nd ed.) and is currently undertaking a 3-year ARC Discovery Project on conspiracy extremism, focusing on sovereign citizen beliefs and behaviours, pseudolaw, and the impact of conspiracy extremism on families and communities.
